As far as exercises go, you mention exercises that work both arms simultaneously. The exercise principle of specificity state "You get what you train for". If you want your one arm to catch up to the other, you need to either work it specifically extra reps or give that arm a heavier weight. I'd stick with the first rather than the second as it's safer.

There are plenty of exercises you can do with one arm. I'd suggest getting a kettle bell which is has a lot of fun enjoyable exercises you can do. But bottom line is that if you want your arm to catch up with the other, it has to put the work in that it lost due to the accident.

This is actually one of my areas of expertise, and while I agree that IDPs as a result of water and food insecurity is going to be a huge problem in the future, you're simplifying this and using incorrect factors to make your determination.

1) The drought wasn't what caused the civil war. It was a contributing factor, but it was the Syrian government killing people which really started the war.

2) Syria's governmental policies are a bigger drive for the drought than anything else. Firstly, their water management policies were poor and unenforced. Unregulated pumping of water resources to be dried up. In reality, water insecurity in the Middle East is discussed very seriously and is believed to be manageable with things like desalinization, better water management policies, and improved infrastructure (fixing leaky pipes for example). Also, Syria's primary food crop is wheat, which is very water intensive.

3) There's nothing wrong with countries buying food with oil money, they've been doing it for years. Oil prices have dropped sharply as a result of fracking, but you can expect oil prices to recover. Oil prices rose sharply in the past, and that was unsustainable. Syria has plenty of hydrocarbons to sell, and also has one of the largest natural gas fields which is yet to be tapped.

4) You can't really compare Syria to other Middle-Eastern nations when it comes to food. Syria had a policy of deeming most food products as "strategic" and forcing producers to sell to the government. Because wheat was one of the few products Syria had that wasn't restricted by sanctions, Syria focused on wheat production in a manner that was unsustainable.

5) There are a ton of things that the Middle-East can do to improve its food and water security. Better management policies, using desalinization, improved water infrastructure, moving to less water intensive food crops, better agricultural technology, etc., etc., etc. To say that the situation now represents what will happen in 5 or 10 years is a logical fallacy.

Do I think we're going to see more refugees in the future? Definitely, but because of things like the increased evaporative capacity of air causing more droughts, which science tells us will happen in arid regions. Not because of a misunderstanding of how oil prices and population impact food security.
